title: Ch 6 — The Second Law of Thermodynamics
source: Cengel, Boles & Kanoglu — Thermodynamics: An Engineering Approach, Ch. 6
description: Heat engines, refrigerators, reversibility, and the Carnot cycle.

cards.back: A body with a very large thermal capacity that can supply or absorb heat without a change in temperature (e.g. oceans, the atmosphere, a furnace). A *source* supplies heat; a *sink* absorbs it.

cards.front: Define the *thermal efficiency* of a heat engine.
cards.back: $\eta_{th} = \dfrac{W_{net,out}}{Q_H} = 1 - \dfrac{Q_L}{Q_H}$, where $Q_H$ is heat received from the source and $Q_L$ heat rejected to the sink.

cards.front: State the *Kelvin–Planck* statement of the second law.
cards.back: No heat engine can convert all the heat it receives into work — it must reject some heat to a low-temperature sink. So thermal efficiency is always less than 100%.

cards.front: State the *Clausius* statement of the second law.
cards.back: Heat cannot, of itself, flow from a colder body to a hotter one. A refrigerator or heat pump requires work input to move heat from low to high temperature.
$COP_R = \dfrac{Q_L}{W_{net,in}} = \dfrac{Q_L}{Q_H - Q_L}$ — desired cooling per unit work input. It can exceed 1.

cards.front: Coefficient of performance of a *heat pump*, and its link to $COP_R$?
*Reversible* vs *irreversible* process — and sources of irreversibility?
cards.back: A reversible process can be undone with no trace left on the system or surroundings; real processes are irreversible. Causes: friction, unrestrained (free) expansion, mixing, and heat transfer across a finite temperature difference.

cards.front: What four processes make up the *Carnot cycle*?
cards.back: All reversible: (1) isothermal heat addition at $T_H$, (2) isentropic (reversible adiabatic) expansion, (3) isothermal heat rejection at $T_L$, (4) isentropic compression.
(1) No engine is more efficient than a reversible engine operating between the same two reservoirs. (2) All reversible engines between the same two reservoirs have the same efficiency.

cards.front: Carnot (reversible) efficiency in terms of temperatures?
cards.back: For a reversible engine $\dfrac{Q_L}{Q_H} = \dfrac{T_L}{T_H}$, so $\eta_{th,rev} = 1 - \dfrac{T_L}{T_H}$ (absolute temperatures, in K).

cards.front: A reversible heat engine operates between 800 K and 300 K. What is its maximum thermal efficiency (as a fraction)?
Which device would violate the second law?
choices: An engine that rejects some heat to a sink
An engine that converts 100% of its heat input into work
A refrigerator driven by work input
A reversible engine between two reservoirs
cards.back: A heat engine converting all received heat into work (no rejection) violates the Kelvin–Planck statement.
